description.narrative: The Fair, Green and Global Alliance (FGG) aims to increase the power and decision-making influence of organised, mobilised and informed civil society, especially women, to advance fair and green trade and value chains. FGG believes that poverty, inequality and exclusion are caused by power asymmetries. We see the unprecedented power of capital over people and planet as the primary obstacle impeding realisation of fair and green trade and value chains. The FGG programme focuses on recalibrating power within the global architecture of trade and value chains by amplifying the voices of targeted rights-holders – small producers and traders, workers, fishers, rural and Indigenous peoples, religious and ethnic minorities, and migrants, especially the women and youth among them – who are practising, claiming or defending human rights and fair and green economic practices, and/or whose rights are being ignored, threatened or violated by corporations and/or governments. We aim to transform social relations so that these rights-holders’ voices are heard and heeded. FGG’s eight members (ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie/Friends of the Earth International/Friends of the Earth Europe, Samdhana Institute, SOMO and the Transnational Institute) cooperate with some 1000+ partners and allies in our many worldwide networks to strengthen collective capacities to advance a common vision of fair and green trade and value chains.

comment.narrative: AA, through a Global South Business and Human Rights coordinator, hosted several learning sessions and events in 2024, for organisations as well as government bodies to raise awareness and build knowledge on the importance of a strong feminist UN Binding treaty for business and human rights, (e.g. the UNBT) and to share information on, and involve CSOs and Global South government representations in, its negotiation process. At community and organisational levels, AA in various countries including in Bangladesh, Kenya, Uganda and Zimbabwe, organized learning sessions on business and human rights in general, and land rights, with a special focus on women’s land rights and internationally agreed standards such as the VGGTs and FPIC. Partners from Guatemala highlight that it is necessary to provide physical, economic and social support to women to facilitate their participation in our work and beyond, since they are the ones who have the most barriers to participate in decision-making spaces. This is important not only for women in the indigenous communities we work with but also for women in the technical teams. Also, participatory cartography has been a fundamental tool for demonstrating human rights violations. By creating thematic maps, it is possible to demonstrate the presence and ancestral rights of indigenous communities over the territory and e.g. identify the historical pattern of expansion of monoculture plantations in the territories. Lastly, ActionAid Netherlands’ 4th Feminist Climate Academy (2024) brought together over 70 young activists from the Netherlands to learn about the climate crisis, possible solutions and how to take action . This resulted in many creative outputs, such as a successful online campaign calling on the Dutch Minister for Climate to pay the climate debt, which was shared widely on social media; a walking tour organized by participants to raise public awareness on the need for gender just climate policies, which the alderwoman of Climate Adaptation in Nijmegen opened and engaged in conversations with visitors on, and the creation by participants of a mini magazine explaining the connection between gender justice and climate justice, which was shared with members of the Dutch government delegation to COP29. An online exchange with young people from the Global South was part of the programme. All the actions together supported our advocacy at COP29 for climate justice, specifically our demand for climate finance for affected communities and the need for gender just climate policies.

In 2023, an in-depth live workshop was held in Kenya in collaboration with SOMO and The Counter, involving over 30 participants from 7 different countries (Bangladesh, Guatemala, Kenya, Uganda, Zimbabwe, South Africa, the Netherlands), where FGG staff and representatives from partner organisations, including community based organisations, gained skills and knowledge on identifying the investors and mother companies abusing environmental, economic and social rights in their areas. This was part of an AA learning trajectory on value chain and supply chain mapping, corporate research and gendered impacts of corporate activities. During the 4 day workshop, participants from the 7 countries also exchanged best practices and lessons learned in relation to supply chain mapping from the cases they currently work on under FGG. This included best practices sharing by AA Bangladesh on mapping fossil energy supply chains through civil society participatory mapping (which they have done through an interactive website); sharing of lessons learned from AA Guatemala on their advocacy strategies towards World Bank/IFC and using the German Due Diligence act based on their mapping of palm oil supply chains; sharing of learning on mapping black granite and gemstone supply chains in secretive contexts in Zimbabwe and knowledge sharing on sugarcane investments and land grabs in Uganda and Kenya.Together with other FGG members, we also hosted an event during the MoFA’s Shaping Feminist Foreign Policy conference in November (see AA’s Narrative on Collaboration with the MoFA) where activists from the Global South shared their visions on what is needed for a Feminist Foreign Policy based on their experiences with the negative social and environmental impacts of mining and other large scale investments.Other topics for joint learning either within countries or among/across countries have included: Feminist Leadership sessions both at grassroots community level, at organisational level and also with external groups; the just energy transition and opportunities for renewable energy. AA hosted several learning sessions and events, both at community and organisational levels, including in Bangladesh, Uganda, Kenya, Guatemala on Binding legislation for business and human rights, (e.g. the UNBT), labour rights, and land rights, with a special focus on women’s land rights and internationally agreed standards such as the VGGTs and FPICLastly, ActionAid’s Feminist Climate Academy brought together activists to learn about the climate crisis and possible solutions.

Together with partners we will engage in offline and online learning sessions both in the Netherlands and in Bangladesh Guatemala Kenya Uganda and Zimbabwe. These learning sessions (both cross-country and country level) will among other things be focused on Land Rights (with special focus on women’s land rights and internationally agreed standards such as the VGGTs and FPIC): the UN Binding Treaty process the Energy Charter Treaty expansion process and risks for countries associated with accession to the Treaty the ActionAid international Campaign on Climate and Agriculture and on Tax Justice. For many of these learning sessions the purpose includes knowledge exchange for shared learning adapting our plans and strategies based on our exchanges but also joint reflection on the programme and how we can strengthen our work based on our joint analysis.

"In FGG-III, ActionAid continues to structurally integrate learning and knowledge exchange between all partners in the programme. Representatives from ActionAid in the five FGG-III focus countries (Bangladesh, Guatemala, Kenya, Uganda and Zimbabwe) as well as in the Netherlands meet bimonthly to jointly discuss emerging opportunities and threats from the changing context, programme risks and mitigation strategies, promising new approaches as well as policy priorities.In 2022, we also organized an Annual Meeting in Zimbabwe. From all five FGG-III focus countries at least one colleague and one partner joined. A field visit was organized to one of the projects, a mining community with women circles to discuss the gendered impacts of the mining activities. The rest of the week we discussed highlights and lessons learned of 2022, strategies and methods and plans for 2023. We also have co-drafted joint work for coming years.Furthermore, we have published joint research on gendered impacts of transnational corporations, with four case studies from Guatemala, Kenya, Uganda and Zimbabwe. The writing and publishing processes have both provided much inside for all involved, and broader. It guides us and our partners in further lobby engagements. The same goes for our joint work and research on the Energy Charter Treaty and on the Dutch Fund for Climate and Development. "

description.narrative: process

comment.narrative: We aim to ensure that all our activities contribute to gender justice in their set up and execution, as well as in their outcomes. We ensure that diverse groups are included in designing, planning and delivering of activities- and also strive for our activities contributing to gender justice. A few examples are named below. At the international level we have also learned that, in relation to Corporate Accountability, there is generally a lack of awareness among most of the CSOs working on this file on the gendered specific impacts of corporate abuse and the need for gender-responsive human rights due diligence. ActionAid as an expert in this area plays an important role in sensitizing civil society in Europe (around the EU CSDDD) and beyond and strengthening the capacity of CSOs to take gender into account when advocating for IRBC policy and legislation. At AA Netherlands we have learned that publishing advocacy briefs targeting both policy makers and civil society is an effective way to strengthen CSO capacity. By doing this in 2022 and 2024 in collaboration with other ActionAid offices (France, Ireland, Spain, Italy, EU), we have been able reach national IRBC coalitions across Europe. In 2024, we published the briefing “Towards a gender-responsive transposition of the CSDDD” in English, French and Spanish and organized two webinars on the outcomes to create awareness among CSOs. Our recommendations were then picked up by other CSO coalitions in their briefings on the CSDDD transposition and recommendations towards policy makers. When it comes to climate justice, AA Netherlands’ continuous engagement with the Dutch Ministry of Climate has shown to help build capacity on gender equality in climate policies. For example, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs invited ActionAid and several other organisations to participate in a workshop with the international climate team to discuss how gender justice can be better integrated into the climate and biodiversity work. This was in response to the joint report we published in September 2024: Fair, sustainable, and effective: Gender equality as a basis for climate and biodiversity policy. Moreover, within civil society organisations working on climate justice there is increased attention for gender equality. Concrete input from CSOs has been welcomed, such as specific recommendations in the report, or textual suggestions for the UNFCCC negotiation texts that we were asked to provide. In 2024 we continued to engage with the Ministry as well as the Dutch development bank (FMO) about our report on the Dutch Fund for Climate and Development (DFCD). We learned that engaging in an open conversation with key stakeholders about critical research findings was valuable, as well as providing space for the stakeholders to share their feedback and incorporate this into the report. This contributed to more effectively getting our message and recommendations across to the DFCD consortium. We also learned that some of our key recommendations on gender inclusion have been incorporated by FMO into their monitoring processes going forward for the second phase of the DFCD.

We aim to ensure that all our activities contribute to gender justice in their set up and execution, as well as in their outcomes. We ensure that diverse groups are included in designing, planning and delivering of activities- and also strive for our activities contributing to gender justice. One example is related to our joint research on DFCD. ActionAid has made ten recommendations to the climate fund, including explicit and measurable gender targets in line with the principles of the recently adopted Feminist Foreign Policy of the Netherlands. the extent to and ways in which FGG involves local groups in the design and implementation of the FGG programme

comment.narrative: Local ownership is intrinsic to AA’s way of working. AA often works bottom up with communities analysing their own context and concerns and prioritizing and planning on actions to be taken. In these cases, AA facilitates community led participatory diagnosis and community led participatory action planning – which means that the actions, activities and campaigns stem from community exercises. By way of concrete examples, in 2024, partners in Zimbabwe trained community members in areas affected by large scale mining as environmental monitors. This is an approach developed by AA’s partner and this has been rolled out as part of FGG in various mining affected communities in Zimbabwe over the past years, whereby AA’s partner ZELA trains people from mining affected communities to identify and document environmental rights violations (in this case, caused by mining operations) to feed into community led advocacy with a view to e.g bringing these cases to court. AA’s partner ZELA also trained people from within mining affected communities to become so-called ‘community paralegals’, to support community members in e.g. filing complaints and bringing cases of corporate abuse to court. In Guatemala, community members affected by palm oil plantations participated in participatory cartography sessions where they were able to map and identify contested territories, areas with heavy pollution and other negative impacts of corporate and industrial activities. Communities in Kenya and Uganda affected by large scale land grabs, forced displacement, and environmental pollution linked to the establishment of sugarcane plantations (Kenya, Uganda) and to salt mining (Kenya) undertook participatory action planning together with AA’s partners in these countries. As a result of these exercises, the communities involved developed plans for advocacy meetings with local government, the sugarcane and salt mining companies or investors involved in the land grabs, to address the violation of their rights to land and property. In Bangladesh, people (women in particular) affected by large scale land grabs, forced displacement, destruction of property and environmental pollution linked to megaprojects for coal power plants came together in women-led Community Land Rights Groups facilitated by ActionAid, to exchange information on their situation and collectively learn about human rights legal frameworks and corporate accountability and plan for action. As a result, communities in three areas across Bangladesh with heavy fossil-based energy investments, designed their own advocacy and campaign actions to demand social justice. This included advocacy meetings with power plant companies and government representatives.

As a result of these exercises, the communities involved developed plans for advocacy meetings with local government, the sugarcane and salt mining companies or investors involved in the land grabs, and for e.g. strategic lawsuits against the violation of their rights to land and property. In Guatemala, communities were trained in and undertook participatory cartography in order to map the environmental and social impacts of mining companies and palm oil plantations, and to get insights into gendered impacts and gender gaps in access to land and water. This fed into their community-led campaigns with e.g. local government to advocate for holding the corporates accountable and guarantee basic rights to the indigenous communities in these territories.In Bangladesh, people (women in particular) affected by large scale land grabs, forced displacement, destruction of property and environmental pollution linked to megaprojects for coal power plants came together in women-led Community Land Rights Groups facilitated by ActionAid, to exchange information on their situation and collectively learn about human rights legal frameworks and corporate accountability and plan for action. As a result, communities in three areas across Bangladesh with heavy fossil based energy investments, designed their own advocacy and campaign actions to demand social justice. This included “human chains”, demonstrations, rallies and advocacy meetings with power plant companies and government representatives.How local ownership is structurally embedded in AA’s way of working in FGGStrategic programme planning (as well as programme budgeting) is fully locally led. To this end, ActionAid has committed to long term partnerships and financial support for FGG’s programme activities in the 5 AA FGG core countries (Bangladesh, Guatemala, Kenya, Uganda, Zimbabwe) for the full duration of FGG-III (2021-2025). This creates a basis for partners in these countries to build strategies for advocacy work with a 5 year time span, and to be able to prioritize where resources are most useful and needed. We believe this long term funding stability is very key in any programme that seeks to be Southern-led and have local ownership. ActionAid offices in these 5 countries consult with their constituencies (NGOs, CBOs, communities, networks and movements in the Global South) and are fully autonomous in identifying their priorities and designing their annual plans within the FGG framework and within agreed accountability guidelines. To strengthen programmatic and strategic links among FGG activities in all countries including The Netherlands, joint bimonthly meetings between all ActionAid offices implementing the FGG programme are held at operational level for continuous sharing of knowledge. ActionAid also facilitates joint annual strategy meetings bringing together our partners in these countries and our team in the Netherlands, in order to collectively identify areas for synergy and complementarity and strengthen connections. Lastly, as part of the ActionAid FGG programme governance structure, an oversight committee bringing together senior leadership from the teams in the Global South is in place for strategic steering of the programme.

In 2022 the FGG programme will also be primarily built upon the expressed needs of our partner organisations and/or on the challenges and opportunities they have identified. This way of working goes well beyond involving or consulting with local groups. Our approach is rather to facilitate for people affected by social injustice to organize and advocate for their rights themselves. We work with AA offices in Bangladesh Guatemala Kenya Uganda and Zimbabwe and their partners (CSOs CBOs and community groups) which are strongly rooted in the communities we support. Therefore they have a key role in defining the ways in which communities are supported and we ensure not only local ownership but local leadership. ActionAid works bottom up and follows the priorities of these local constituents in the design of local and national level programmes. In 2022 all countries will build on the track record from FGG-II supporting communities affected by large scale investments (in mining agribusiness energy projects) to advocate for their rights and for remedy in cases where these rights have been violated. We will collaborate with these partners to shed light on local cases in research publications as well as in lobby meetings in which partners will participate directly including in international policymaking fora and lobby meetings targeting national or local decision makers. We will continue to mobilize and facilitate the organization of community groups in e.g. in Bangladesh where the setting up of over 90 Community Land Rights groups in FGG-2 was a highly successful strategy to engage vulnerable communities affected by large scale energy infrastructure projects and support them to take center stage in advocating for their rights. In Kenya and Uganda too we will continue our work with community and women’s groups on land rights and support community- and women-led advocacy for land and other rights. In e.g. Guatemala some communities will receive additional training for enhanced mobilization and participation e.g. in (inter)national decision-making spaces and other communities will start being involved in the FGG programme to lobby and advocate for their own rights.

"The expansion of the Energy Charter Treaty to Bangladesh, Kenya and Uganda is likely further away as a result of the efforts of our partner organisations in those countries. The ECT secretariat is pushing for the treaty to expand to other countries, mostly in the global South. Accession makes these countries vulnerable to claims that stand in the way of the energy transition. In 2022, meetings were organized with our colleagues and partners in Bangladesh Kenya and Uganda, with experts (TNI) and with AANL. The ECT in general and its impacts were discussed extensively. Based on these meetings, colleagues and partners in these countries started research and lobby efforts. First steps were taken to draw attention to the dangers of accession. In Uganda, the country that had progressed the farthest in preparing accession to the treaty, this has already led to an informal statement by a key government official that Uganda will not accede to the Treaty. In Bangladesh, so far also preparing to join the treaty, strong civil society movement against the Treaty has already taken shape. While the ECT was completely unknown in Bangladesh before, it is now widely discussed in the media, among politicians and in academia and civil society. Also in regard of the UN Binding treaty of Business and Human Rights, capacities have been strengthened in several countries (Bangladesh, Kenya, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Guatemala) and in multiple communities. Together with our ActionAid counterparts we have strategized on how to improve our lobby on the UNBT. We decided to publish a joint report, with feminist recommendations based on case studies in four countries (Kenya, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Guatemala). These cases show the gendered impacts of transnational corporations in host communities. All countries conducted their own research and wrote their cases. Together we created the joint report, worked on joint recommendations and strategized a dissemination plan. Together we lobbied in Geneva during the negotiations, and separately all ‘owners‘ of the report lobbied in their respective countries and organized trainings and validation sessions in the related communities. It was the first time that ActionAid engaged in the topic. The current platform includes organisations from inside and outside FGG in Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America. As a result of knowledge sharing and joint strategizing, organisations in countries including in Bangladesh and Kenya have for the first-time developed action plans to start advocacy work in their countries to generate awareness both with policy makers and in civil society on the risks for their country associated with accession to the Treaty. At the time of writing, research projects as a basis for advocacy and awareness raising work in the first half of 2022 are under way for AA in Bangladesh, Uganda and Kenya (3). This is significant, as so far, the Energy Charter Treaty and its expansion agenda were little known in the countries in the platform. At the same time, the ECT expansion process poses serious risks for candidate countries, including in terms of their ability to address e.g. negative impacts of energy related infrastructure projects or to take climate action in the future.
